**Ch 006 draft scan**

The draft compresses the Carter meeting and the Hersheimmer lunch competently. One potential issue:

> "Ow! That's enough!"

In the draft the pinch request ("Pinch me, Tommy, do pinch me") is present, but the beat between is cut so that "Ow! That's enough!" appears as an isolated exclamation with no clear speaker attribution or trigger visible — but re-reading the draft, the sequence is: Tuppence says "Pinch me… I can't believe it's real!" followed immediately by "Ow! That's enough!" A competent reader infers she is responding to being pinched. Not a genuine confusion.

The transition to the Ritz lunch is abrupt — the draft jumps from the taxi/extravagance banter to "On inquiring for Mr. Hersheimmer at the *Ritz*" cutting the intermediate banter — but the Ritz is named, so no mid-scene jump.

The jump to "Oysters had just given place to Sole Colbert" is a mid-scene cut — in the source Julius proposes lunch, Tuppence chooses the restaurant, and they go. The draft omits all of this. But does the lunch scene reference something from the cut material? No — "Oysters had just given place to Sole Colbert" is self-explanatory. Not a finding.

One genuine issue: the draft cuts Mr. Hersheimmer's statement that he thought the British might be after Jane "for contempt of court or something British" and Tuppence's reassurance, then jumps directly to:

> "Scotland Yard again. Another man. I hope they haven't lost that photograph. The Western photographer's place was burned down and his negatives destroyed—this is the only copy in existence."

In the source, before this line, Julius has invited them to lunch, they've gone to the restaurant, and the Inspector Japp card arrives. But the draft has no transition at all from Hersheimmer's narration to the lunch scene — "Oysters had just given place to Sole Colbert" appears without any establishment of the lunch happening. The question is whether the previous draft established the lunch. Looking back: the draft has Hersheimmer say "I'm off to Paris to-morrow" and then immediately: "Oysters had just given place to Sole Colbert when a card was brought to Hersheimmer." The lunch is not established in the draft — there is no invitation, no acceptance, no movement to a restaurant. However, a competent reader would understand they are eating lunch together; the Sole Colbert line is self-contextualizing. This falls under "temporal sequencing is slightly altered but still parses" — the reader knows they're at lunch. Not a finding.

The card scene itself: "Scotland Yard again. Another man." The "again" refers to the Scotland Yard visit that morning — which IS established in the draft ("Scotland Yard were very civil—even sent a man round this morning"). So "again" parses. Fine.

No valid findings in Ch 006.

**Ch 007 draft scan**

The draft opens cleanly. The rapprochement is established, the move to the Ritz is explained. The campaign planning scene compresses well.

One candidate:

> "She set out her reasoning: the man Danvers had been shadowed on the way over, very likely by a woman, a good-looking one."

"Danvers" — is this name established anywhere in the preceding draft? In Ch 007 draft it appears here for the first time. In Ch 007 source, Tuppence says "That man, Danvers, was shadowed on the way over." In the Ch 006 draft, there is no mention of Danvers. Is Danvers established in any earlier draft chapter that a reader of the abridgment would have seen? This is Chapter 7; the name Danvers would have been introduced in a prior chapter (in the source novel, Danvers is the man who carried the papers on the Lusitania and was murdered). If the abridgment's earlier chapters established Danvers, this is fine. Since we only have Ch 006 and Ch 007, and "Danvers" does not appear in Ch 006 draft, the question is whether it was established in an even earlier chapter. We cannot confirm this from the supplied material, and the gate test asks whether a reader would be *genuinely confused*. A reader who has read the earlier abridgment chapters would know Danvers; this is mid-novel context. This is not a mid-scene jump (that test is about chapter-opening definite references cut from the *immediately preceding* chapter). Danvers is not a chapter-opening reference. This is a missing antecedent only if the reader has never encountered the name — which depends on earlier chapters not supplied. I cannot flag this as a finding based on available material.

The more significant candidate:

> "Quick—follow them. I daren't. He might recognize me. The bigger of the two was Whittington."

In the source: "I don't know who the other man is, but the bigger of the two was Whittington." The draft cuts "I don't know who the other man is, but" — leaving only "The bigger of the two was Whittington." This is a truncation but the sentence still parses and conveys the essential fact. Not a finding.

The draft cuts the "first port of call" / discouragement exchange before South Audley Mansions but retains the discouragement line ("Tommy, I'm getting discouraged") and Tommy's response. Does this create a broken pivot? Tommy says "Buck up, old bean. We always knew it was an outside chance." This is a response to Tuppence's discouragement, which IS present in the draft. No broken pivot.

One genuine structural issue:

> "She set out her reasoning: the man Danvers had been shadowed on the way over, very likely by a woman, a good-looking one. That woman must have been saved—else how would they have known Jane Finn had the papers? With luck, she might be Rita."

The draft narrates this in indirect free discourse, which works. But "With luck, she might be Rita" — "Rita" has been introduced two sentences earlier ("Only a Christian name—Rita"). This parses. Fine.

Another candidate — the notebook/list:

> "Tuppence produced Mr. Carter's reply enclosing the official statement of those saved."

In the source, Tuppence explains she "wrote a long list of things I wanted to know, and sent it to Mr. Carter." The draft cuts this backstory. But "Mr. Carter's reply" is sufficient — Carter was established in Ch 006 as their handler. A reader understands she contacted him. Not a finding.

The closing sequence: "There were footsteps on the stairs above, and voices. Suddenly Tuppence dragged him into the shadow beside the lift." In the source: "the little space by the side of the lift where the shadow was deepest." The draft says "the shadow beside the lift" — slightly less precise but parseable. Not a finding.

After careful analysis, I find no sentences that fail the gate test — no genuine structural damage where a competent reader would be confused or misled rather than simply reading a less-ornamented version.
